extracted.intended_audience: astronomers and observatory observers/reducers performing solar and lunar meridional observations and reductions (observatory assistants, instrument operators)
extracted.subtask_short: reducing astronomical solar and lunar observations
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and reduction standards for meridional, solar, and lunar observations (solstices, transits, repetitions) including choice of reduction series, corrections to apply (equation of time, nutation, sun's latitude), observational technique (direct vs reflection), and methods for longitude determination by comparison with the Nautical Almanac.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to the Meridian (alternative to Delambre)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the sun culminates near the zenith Delambre's method converges slowly; substitute another series whose very first term approximates the truth as closely as Delambre's four terms. Take the middle of the times of observation and compute the required parts (A, A', A" ...) for each individual time; form means and compute reduction R according to the derived formula (R = II S — p2 cotang. *(...)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page gives a step-by-step derivation: call the different unknown zenith distances available, form means, introduce q = 2p cot £ sin l" etc., and resolve by binomial theorem. Use the substituted series because when the hour-angle is about 25' Delambre's second, third, and fourth terms become large and laborious. The author provides the algebraic demonstration and explicit series terms to implement the alternative reduction to the meridian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation and omission rules in meridian reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: In the reduction to the meridian some higher-order terms are 'almost always insensible' and may be neglected; an observed zenith distance may be used in place of an unknown term without introducing more than about one second of arc error provided the reduction is not above two degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit cubes and higher powers where justified. The author quantifies that the approximations used cause an error of at most one second of arc in the reduction as long as the reduction is not above two degrees. This gives a practical tolerance for neglecting small terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of the Hour-angle for change of Equation of Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct the observed hour-angle (apparent solar time) for the daily rate of the clock and for the daily difference of equation of time (given in the Nautical Almanac).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biot corrected only for daily rate of clock but neglected the daily difference of equation of time, which can be larger (e.g. gaining late of the clock of 13" in the northern but 30" in the southern solstice). These corrections are important where zenith distance is small: an error of 1" in the hour-angle of 24 minutes can cause an error of 10" in latitude. The author supplies a table of corrections (hours -> arcseconds) to be subtracted from hour-angle during the southern solstice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of Hour-angle to Sidereal Time (daily RA difference correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: When converting an hour-angle (apparent solar time) to sidereal time, decrease or increase it by a proportional part of the daily difference of apparent solar time upon mean time (or equivalently, depending on whether daily difference of right ascension is less or more than 3'56.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the proportional adjustment according to whether the apparent time is gaining or losing upon mean time; this is equivalent to using the daily difference of right ascension relative to 3'56.6 in the conversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of the assumed time of the Sun's culmination
rubrics_metrics.description: If meridional altitudes deduced from an assumed time of culmination form a monotonically increasing or decreasing set, the assumed transit time is in error; compute the correction using the differences among ascending and descending meridional altitudes and the Delambre table quantities for change per one second in time (m and n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: take mean of Delambre's numbers A for an ascending set and for a descending set; take from his Tables the quantities corresponding to a change of one second in time (m for ascending mean A and n for descending mean) and then compute the time error x using the formula given (A - E etc.). Apply the correction (A - m x = E + n x etc.) to obtain the true meridional altitude. The author notes the correction for change of declination should already be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to the Solstice (formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute reduction to the solstice after the formula = C × sinHL, where the constant c = L (complement of the sun's longitude), D is the declination, and co is the obliquity of the ecliptic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified formula with the defined constants to reduce observed meridional zenith distances to the solstice. The author applies this in the tabulated solstice reductions and uses lunar-solar nutation and reductions to the year's commencement as further corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of observing repetitions (use of reflection from mercury)
rubrics_metrics.description: When observing repetitions (repeated altitudes/zenith distances), use reflection from a mercury nadir placed on the same isolated pillar as the instrument, keep the dome openings shut except the top slide, and avoid revolving the instrument 180° in azimuth during a series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method secures the mercury against wind and minimizes percussion to only handling. The observer points the tube first to the reflected image using the great circle, then shifts the small circle to the direct object and repeats, alternating reflected and direct observations until a series is completed. No glass cover is required; the small nadir distance allows placing the mercury on the same pillar as the instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series ordering and instrument-stability requirement for reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: In left-sided series point the tube to the reflected image first by the great circle, then to the direct object by shifting the small circle; in right-sided series reverse the order. During the interval between reflected and direct vision the instrument must remain steady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the left/right-sided protocol so repetitions can be carried on with remarkable expedition by one observer. Instrument steadiness during the interval is required so that reflection and direct vision allow verification that the optical axis describes a vertical circle and that bending effects compensate themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reflection to enable one-observer repetition and to verify optical axis
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection and direct vision enable a single observer, by three observations, to verify that the optical axis describes a vertical circle and that effects of bending compensate themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author illustrates the process with an example and shows that using reflected/direct sequence reduces manpower needs while providing checks on instrument alignment and bending.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to prefer reflection over attending the level
rubrics_metrics.description: In the southern solstice, attending simultaneously to the level causes large interval corrections (second parts of reductions p2 cot z (s — &)) and becomes impractical when the sun is near vertical; therefore prefer reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection avoids needing to revolve instrument or attend level during the series, reducing the second-part corrections and allowing faster observation when the sun is vertical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of small corrections in the second part of reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The second part of the reduction depends on distance from meridian, number of observations in the set, and intervals. Small corrections that have variable signs and complete their periods during the observation set may be neglected; small corrections with constant sign must be attended to since their error won't be diminished by averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only variable-sign small corrections that average out over the set can be neglected; when sign is constant even the smallest corrections should be applied because means won't reduce that systematic error and repeated observations won't help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of corrections with proper signs for solstice reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrections for sun's latitude, reduction to solstice, luni-solar nutation, and reductions to the commencement of the year must be applied with signs adapted for finding the zenith distance of the mean tropic: the correction for the sun's latitude is applied with the opposite sign; luni-solar nutation in the southern solstice is applied with the same sign, but in the northern solstice with the opposite sign to what the solar tables give.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about sign conventions: the author emphasizes to avoid misconstruction by stating the sign rules he used across his sols tice reductions and tabulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitude determination by lunar culminations compared to Nautical Almanac
rubrics_metrics.description: From known right ascensions of the Moon’s culminating stars (observed) deduce the true right ascension of the Moon’s centre at the apparent time of limb passage; find the Moon’s right ascension at the corresponding Greenwich time from the Nautical Almanac (with appropriate corrections); the difference divided by the Moon’s horary motion yields the error of the assumed longitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author computes RA at Paramatta and at Greenwich (assuming an initial longitude), applies corrections from Greenwich observations, and divides the RA difference by the Moon's hourly motion (which need only be known superficially) to get the longitude error. He notes sign conventions for east longitude (additive or subtractive depending on whether Almanac RA is greater or less than observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying Almanac error corrections to longitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: The longitudes found by comparison with the Nautical Almanac rest on that comparison; when the Almanac errors are once known, apply double those quantities to the longitudes in time found on the corresponding days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prescribes doubling the Almanac errors as corrections to the time-longitudes calculated from lunar comparisons once Almanac errors are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Averaging multiple longitude determinations and handling outliers
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a mean of all calculated observations (including occupations and chronometric determinations), but exercise judgement to reject clearly faulty results (e.g., results from the beginning of an event) and prefer a mean excluding such outliers; the author prefers taking a mean of several determinations rather than relying on a single phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: various determinations between Paramatta and Sydney produced 51"93, 51"98, and 49"6; the author prefers to reject the beginning results of one series and take a mean of selected values (or a mean of all hitherto calculated observations) to produce the final adopted longitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of reduction method depending on hour-angle magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Delambre's method is insufficient when the hour-angle is small (about 25'); its terms produce large contributions and are laborious — therefore substitute a more rapidly converging series whose first term approximates the combined effect of many of Delambre's terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the hour-angle before selecting reduction approach; for small hour-angles use the alternative series derived by the author to obtain faster convergence and less laborious calculation.
